headline: AMD and Cerebras Split AI Inference in Two — Read the Footnote
headings: Read the footnote before the headline number
Two jobs, two very different machines
The hop between them is the engineering
This lands harder for Cerebras than for AMD
Cloud-first means you cannot buy it yet
Splitting inference is already ordinary
How to test the claim when it ships
What would change this read
Frequently asked questions
Comments
paragraphs: This article covers product and infrastructure announcements from publicly traded companies. It is technology analysis, not investment advice, and nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

If you serve agent workloads and you take only the headline out of San Francisco this afternoon, you will walk away with the wrong number in your head. AMD and Cerebras say their new joint inference system is expected to deliver up to 5x higher tokens per second per watt. The footnote underneath that claim says the comparison is against a Cerebras-only configuration. Not against Nvidia . Not against an AMD rack on its own. Not against whatever you are running in production today.

The engineering behind the announcement is genuinely interesting, and it points at something the whole inference market has been circling for a year. The number attached to it is narrower than it looks.

The joint release went out at 1:45 p.m. Eastern on Thursday, from AMD's San Francisco event and Cerebras's Sunnyvale headquarters. It describes a disaggregated inference system: AMD Helios rackscale hardware handles prompt processing and large context windows, and the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine handles the memory-bandwidth-intensive job of generating tokens.

Both companies publish the same performance line, and both publish the same qualifier . The 5x figure comes from modelling by AMD Performance Labs and Cerebras in July 2026, measuring tokens per second per kilowatt at a comparable interactivity point on the Kimi 2.6 1T model, comparing an AMD Helios rackscale solution paired with Cerebras WSE against a Cerebras WSE-only configuration.
That qualifier does a lot of work:

None of that makes the claim dishonest. Both companies disclosed the basis clearly, which is more than a lot of AI infrastructure marketing manages. It does mean the number cannot be lifted out of the release and compared against a GPU quote from anyone else.
Serving a large language model is not one workload. It is two, and they stress hardware in opposite directions.

The first stage reads your prompt: the system instructions, the retrieved documents, the tool output, the earlier turns of the conversation. That work is dense matrix multiplication across the whole input at once. It saturates compute units and it scales with how much text you sent.

The second stage writes the answer, one token at a time. Each new token requires re-reading the model weights and the accumulated key-value cache. Very little new arithmetic happens per token; the machine spends its time moving data. That stage is bound by memory bandwidth, and it is what a user experiences as speed.

Cerebras built its business on the second half. Keeping weights in enormous on-wafer SRAM sidesteps the bandwidth wall that constrains token generation on conventional accelerators. What a wafer-scale part is not built for is the first half at scale — chewing through very long contexts, where raw dense throughput and memory capacity matter more than latency.

AMD's answer to that half is a rack. The Helios configuration AMD detailed at the same event pairs 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs with 18 sixth-generation EPYC CPUs and Pensando networking, and AMD says it is now in production. TECHi looked at the economics of that rack-as-a-product model when Helios was first laid out, and the shape of it has not changed: AMD sells the whole box, not the chip.

Put the two together and each part runs the stage it was designed for. That is the actual claim, and it is a defensible one — independent of whether the number attached to it survives contact with a real workload.
There is a cost to splitting the work, and neither release quantifies it.

When prefill and decode run on separate machines, the key-value cache produced by the first stage has to reach the second stage before the first token can be emitted. Inside a single vendor's fabric, that transfer rides a purpose-built interconnect. Here it crosses not just machines but architectures — GPU high-bandwidth memory on one side, wafer-scale SRAM on the other, two different memory models and two different software stacks.

For short prompts, the cache is small and the hop is cheap. For the long contexts that agent systems actually generate — accumulated tool results, retrieved documents, multi-turn history — the cache is large, and every millisecond spent moving it comes straight out of the latency advantage the partnership is selling. The rise in raw token demand over the past year has pushed context lengths up, not down.

The releases name the two engines and the efficiency claim. They do not name the interconnect, the transfer mechanism, or the measured penalty at any context length. That is the number a buyer will eventually need, and it is the one that is missing.
Read the two announcements side by side and the asymmetry is obvious.

For Cerebras, this fills a hole in the product. The company's pitch has always been speed, and its exposure has always been everything upstream of speed. The partnership also comes with a purchase: Cerebras plans to deploy AMD Helios systems in its own data centres. It is buying prefill capacity rather than building it into silicon. When TECHi looked at who was actually buying Cerebras capacity after its first quarter as a public company, concentration was the open question. Widening the workload envelope is a direct response to that.

For AMD, Cerebras is one name on a long list. The full-stack release published 45 minutes later put Anthropic on stage for up to 2 gigawatts of MI450-series GPUs in Helios racks, OpenAI with Helios systems expected online in the fourth quarter, and Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, AT&T and Cisco alongside them. A wafer-scale partner is a useful proof point for AMD's argument that inference is diversifying. It is not load-bearing for the business.

Worth noting for anyone modelling the roadmap rather than the quarter: AMD also put MI500 in 2027 and MI600 in 2028 on the record at the same event. The cadence is now annual, and the parts announced this week are already the near end of it.
The system becomes available in the second half of 2026, initially through Cerebras Cloud. There is no on-premises SKU, no listed price, and no self-hosted path in either announcement.

That matters more than it sounds. A large share of the teams most attracted to ultra-low-latency inference are the ones who cannot send their tokens to someone else's data centre — regulated industries, defence-adjacent work, anyone with a residency constraint. For those teams the interesting design pattern remains a self-hosted serving stack, where the operational questions are authentication, isolation and air-gapped deployment rather than tokens per watt. Nothing announced on Thursday reaches them.
If you can use a hosted endpoint, the relevant metric will not be watts at all. It will be dollars per million tokens on Cerebras Cloud, at your context length, against whatever you pay now.
Disaggregated serving is not new, and it is worth being precise about what is.

Nvidia shipped Dynamo 1.0 in March, an open-source serving layer whose headline feature is routing prefill and decode to separate worker pools , with a dedicated library for shuttling KV caches between them. vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM all support the pattern. Large providers have run it in production for a while. Any serving team that has tuned a fleet this year has already met the idea.

What is new here is doing it across two different classes of accelerator built by two different companies — a GPU rack in front, a wafer-scale engine behind. That is harder than splitting across two pools of identical GPUs, and it is also a quiet admission from both vendors that no single part is the right shape for both halves of the job. The efficiency framing is part of the same shift: per-watt and per-megawatt economics are becoming the unit of comparison as power, not silicon, turns into the binding constraint on capacity.
If this system is on your evaluation list for later this year, the useful questions are narrow ones:
Any vendor that can answer those six is selling something real. The 5x, on its own, is not an answer to any of them.

The skepticism here is about disclosure, not about the architecture. If AMD and Cerebras publish measured results — multiple models, multiple context lengths, a mainstream GPU baseline, ideally a third-party harness — and the efficiency ratio holds up anywhere near five, then the caution in this piece was about a press release rather than a product, and the split-machine approach becomes the reference design for latency-sensitive serving rather than an experiment.

The reverse case is just as plausible. If the transfer penalty at long context turns out to eat most of the gain, disaggregation stays inside single-vendor fabrics where the interconnect is controlled end to end, and this partnership ends up remembered as a capacity deal — Cerebras buying racks it needed — with an efficiency chart attached.
Second half of 2026 is when that resolves. Until then, the sentence to keep in mind is the one in the footnote, not the one in the headline.

headline: Amazon's $20B chip pace turns AI capacity into a supply contract
headings: What Amazon actually disclosed
Why sold-out silicon changes the buyer's math
What triple-digit growth actually implies
The constraint behind the constraint
Where this leaves the GPU incumbents
What a capacity buyer should actually do
The honest bottom line
Frequently asked questions
Comments
paragraphs: Amazon put a number on its chip business this spring, and the number is doing quiet damage to a common assumption: that AI training capacity is something you rent when you need it. On the company's first-quarter earnings call, CEO Andy Jassy said Amazon's custom silicon line — the Trainium AI accelerators, Graviton CPUs and Nitro networking chips inside AWS — is now generating revenue at an annual pace above $20 billion, after growing nearly 40% in a single quarter. Buyers have responded by locking up more than $225 billion in multi-year Trainium commitments. Capacity that used to be a monthly bill is being bought like a supply contract.
That shift, more than the headline figure, is what anyone budgeting for AI compute needs to sit with.
The disclosures came from Jassy's own commentary on the Q1 2026 call , and the specifics matter more than the totals.

The $20 billion run rate covers the whole custom silicon family, growing at triple-digit percentages year over year. Jassy's framing went further: if the unit sold chips to third parties the way Nvidia or Broadcom do, he put its standalone pace at roughly $50 billion — his basis for calling it one of the top three data center chip businesses in operation.

The backdrop gives the number scale. The disclosure landed in a quarter where AWS itself re-accelerated to $37.6 billion in revenue, up 28% year over year — its fastest growth in 15 quarters — which means the chip line is compounding faster than the already-compounding cloud around it.

Then the supply side. Trainium2, which Amazon prices at about 30% better price-performance than comparable GPU instances, has largely sold out. Trainium3 , shipping since the start of 2026 at another 30–40% price-performance step over Trainium2, is nearly fully subscribed. Trainium4 is still around 18 months from broad availability — and much of it is already reserved.
Read those three sentences together and the picture is stark: the current chip is gone, the new chip is nearly gone, and the chip that does not exist yet is spoken for.

A $225 billion commitment book is not how companies buy cloud services. It is how airlines buy fuel and utilities buy gas — forward contracts against a scarce input. Training capacity is now being treated as supply insurance, and insurance always carries a premium and a counterparty.

The premium here is flexibility. A team that signs a multi-year Trainium reservation is betting that Amazon's price-performance ladder keeps climbing on schedule. Two rungs are on record so far — roughly 30% from GPU instances to Trainium2, another 30–40% to Trainium3. If Trainium4 lands on time, committed buyers ride the curve at locked economics. If it slips, they hold reservations on yesterday's chip while rivals shop the spot market.

The counterparty question is concentration. Every dollar in that commitment book deepens dependence on one vendor's roadmap, one instance family, and one software stack. Porting a training pipeline off a custom accelerator is measured in engineering quarters, not config changes. That is the same lock-in logic TECHi traced in the tokens-per-megawatt arms race — efficiency claims are real, but they bind you to the claimant.

There is also a gap worth naming in what Jassy did not say. The $50 billion standalone framing assumes selling to third parties, yet Amazon made no commitment to becoming a merchant chip vendor. Until that changes, Trainium economics are only reachable one way: through AWS. The comparison to Nvidia is therefore not apples to apples — one sells chips anywhere, the other sells a destination.

Growth claims deserve arithmetic, so here is the arithmetic — clearly labeled as arithmetic, not forecast. A business at a $20 billion annual pace growing "triple digit percentages year-over-year," in Jassy's words, implies a pace somewhere above $40 billion within a year if the rate merely holds at its floor. That is how a $225 billion commitment book stops looking irrational: at those rates, today's book is a few years of forward revenue, not a decade's.

The same arithmetic explains the urgency on the other side of the table. Every quarter a buyer waits, the queue for constrained generations lengthens and the entry point moves. Waiting is a position, and right now it is a position with a visible cost.

Two cautions keep this honest. Growth rates measured off newly disclosed bases have a habit of decelerating once the base matures — nearly 40% quarter-over-quarter is a launch-curve number, not a steady state. And run rate is an annualized snapshot, not booked revenue; it inherits every seasonal and mix quirk of the quarter it annualizes. The direction is unambiguous. The slope, further out, is not.

Sold-out silicon is only half the scarcity story. Chips need buildings, and buildings need power. Grid connection queues and utility fights are already shaping where AI capacity can physically exist, a dynamic TECHi mapped in its look at data centers and electricity bills . A reserved accelerator that cannot be energized is a receipt, not capacity.

That is why the $225 billion book reads less like exuberance and more like triage. Buyers are not just paying for FLOPs; they are paying to be first in line when constrained chips meet constrained megawatts. For Amazon , the commitments de-risk a capital program Jassy has defended as demand-driven rather than speculative. For everyone else, they raise the cost of waiting.

None of this reads as a GPU obituary, and pretending otherwise would flunk the same honesty test applied above. Jassy's own benchmark — 30% better price-performance than "comparable GPUs" — concedes the comparison class: general-purpose accelerators remain the default that custom silicon must beat, workload by workload. Frameworks, kernels and hiring pipelines still assume them. A research lab iterating on novel architectures has good reasons to pay the GPU premium for flexibility that a custom part cannot offer.

What the disclosure does change is the shape of the negotiation. A top-three data center chip business growing inside the largest cloud gives every serious buyer a credible second bid — and second bids discipline pricing even when they lose. The pressure lands asymmetrically: hardest on undifferentiated GPU capacity resold through clouds, least on the frontier parts that stay supply-constrained on their own merits. In between sits a widening band of workloads where the question "why not Trainium?" now needs a written answer.

The unresolved variable is still distribution. As long as Amazon's chips are reachable only inside AWS, the incumbents keep the whole rest of the market by default. That is a real moat — and a reminder that the standalone $50 billion framing describes a business Amazon could run, not one it does.

The practical response is not "sign faster." It is pricing the trade honestly, the way a procurement team would price any long-dated supply contract with a single counterparty. Four moves cover most of the ground.

Amazon disclosed a chip business at a $20 billion pace, growing triple digits, with three generations of capacity effectively spoken for. Those are verified numbers with a named source, and they justify taking custom silicon seriously as the second pole of AI compute.

The disclosure also resets how competing claims should be read. When a cloud vendor reports its accelerator sold out through generations that have not shipped, GPU scarcity narratives and custom-silicon scarcity narratives stop being alternatives and start being the same story told from two directions: demand for AI training capacity is outrunning every supply chain that feeds it, at once.

What the numbers do not settle is whether pre-committing years of capacity to one vendor's roadmap is prudence or exposure. That answer depends on the buyer: how portable the workload is, how much roadmap risk the budget can absorb, and how expensive waiting really is. The companies writing $225 billion in commitments have decided waiting is the bigger risk. It is a defensible bet. It is not a free one.

For readers tracking the companies rather than the capacity, the watch-list writes itself: whether the next earnings call updates the run rate or lets the number age, whether Trainium4's 18-month clock holds, and whether the word "merchant" ever enters Amazon's vocabulary. Each of those is a checkable fact with a date attached — which is exactly the kind of claim this story was built on, and the kind worth waiting for before anyone updates the thesis.
FAQ

On the Q1 2026 earnings call, CEO Andy Jassy said Amazon's custom silicon business — Trainium, Graviton, and Nitro — has passed a $20 billion annual revenue run rate, growing nearly 40% quarter-over-quarter and at triple-digit percentages year over year.

Jassy disclosed that customers have signed more than $225 billion in multi-year revenue commitments for Trainium capacity — forward contracts that reserve future chip generations rather than pay-as-you-go cloud usage.

No. Amazon has made no commitment to selling Trainium as a merchant chip vendor; Jassy's roughly $50 billion standalone figure was a hypothetical framing. Trainium economics are currently reachable only through AWS instances.

Per Amazon's Q1 2026 commentary, Trainium2 has largely sold out, Trainium3 began shipping at the start of 2026 with a 30–40% price-performance improvement and is nearly fully subscribed, and Trainium4 — about 18 months from broad availability — is already largely reserved.

This article is for information only and is not investment advice. Figures are company-reported and dated to Amazon's Q1 2026 earnings call; verify current data before making capacity or investment decisions.

That answer depends on the buyer: how portable the workload is, how much roadmap risk the budget can absorb, and how expensive waiting really is. The companies writing $225 billion in commitments have decided waiting is the bigger risk. It is a defensible bet. It is not a free one. For readers tracking the companies rather than the capacity, the watch-list writes itself: whether the next earnings call updates the run rate or lets the number age, whether Trainium4's 18-month clock holds, and whether the word "merchant" ever enters Amazon's vocabulary. Each of those is a checkable fact with a date attached — which is exactly the kind of claim this story was built on, and the kind worth waiting for before anyone updates the thesis. FAQ On the Q1 2026 earnings call, CEO Andy Jassy said Amazon's custom silicon business — Trainium, Graviton, and Nitro — has passed a $20 billion annual revenue run rate, growing nearly 40% quarter-over-quarter and at triple-digit percentages year over year. Jassy disclosed that customers have signed more than $225 billion in multi-year revenue commitments for Trainium capacity — forward contracts that reserve future chip generations rather than pay-as-you-go cloud usage. No. Amazon has made no commitment to selling Trainium as a merchant chip vendor; Jassy's roughly $50 billion standalone figure was a hypothetical framing. Trainium economics are currently reachable only through AWS instances. Per Amazon's Q1 2026 commentary, Trainium2 has largely sold out, Trainium3 began shipping at the start of 2026 with a 30–40% price-performance improvement and is nearly fully subscribed, and Trainium4 — about 18 months from broad availability — is already largely reserved. headline: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion Over Facebook Privacy Deceptions
headings: What the judge decided
The penalty math
Eleven years of statements
The investigation that wasn't
Why $25 billion, not $219.5 billion
A second legal bill
What to watch
Comments
paragraphs: Meta's headquarters in Menlo Park, California. Photo: InvadingInvader via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

A New Mexico judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for systematically misleading Facebook users about their privacy, after a jury found 43.9 million willful violations of state law. The judge ruled $219.5 billion was warranted but reduced the award; the state had sought up to $40 billion.

The order, filed Wednesday morning in state district court in Santa Fe, ends the penalty phase of a case New Mexico filed in 2021 in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica revelations — the first state-led case of its kind to reach a jury verdict. By law, the money goes to New Mexico's schools, and at $25 billion it is more than twice the state's entire annual budget.

The 20-page judgment, filed at 10:51 a.m. on October 21 in the First Judicial District Court for Santa Fe County, converts the jury's September verdict into money. The jury had found that Meta committed 43,899,720 willful violations through unfair or deceptive trade practices, plus five more through willful unconscionable trade practices — 43,899,725 willful violations in total.

New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act allows up to $5,000 per violation. At that ceiling, the arithmetic the court adopted is exact: 43,899,720 × $5,000 = $219,498,600,000. The judge concluded that figure was warranted — then cut it to $25 billion. Interest runs at 15% a year until Meta pays, and the court reserved any injunctive relief for later briefing, which means court-ordered changes to Facebook's products remain on the table.

The New Mexico Department of Justice called it one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in U.S. history. The full judgment — findings of fact, conclusions of law and the penalty order — is published on the department's site.

Three ratios put the number in perspective. The $25 billion is about 11% of what the judge found warranted — a steep reduction, but still five times the $5 billion FTC penalty from 2019, the previous record for the same Cambridge Analytica scandal. It equals roughly two and a half quarters of Meta's reported profit — the company earned $9.86 billion in the third quarter — and about 12% of the $200.97 billion in 2025 revenue cited in the judgment. And at 15%, the interest meter alone adds $3.75 billion a year while Meta appeals, nearly 40% of a quarter's profit annually, before a dollar of the principal is touched.

The violations were not a single incident. The 26 representations the jury found unlawful and willful span more than eleven years, from May 24, 2010 through August 18, 2021, and they were made through Facebook's own platform, its newsroom, earnings calls, national television and print interviews, and public conferences. The expected audience for each statement was either Facebook's 1,386,648 monthly active users in New Mexico or the state's roughly 2.1 million residents — that audience math is how 26 statements became 43.9 million violations.

Among the speakers were Facebook's most senior leaders, including chief executive Mark Zuckerberg and then-chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg. The court found the communications were "part of a coherent strategy designed to mislead the public," citing internal messaging materials — called a "song sheet" — used to coordinate external messaging across company representatives and forums. In one instance, an internal communication to Zuckerberg himself warned that proposed public communications were misleading.

A private email from Zuckerberg to another senior executive, shown at trial, captured the internal view of users: that they "probably don't understand their current privacy settings or care about who sees their updates" — and laid out a plan to change those settings without users noticing, rolling features out so that "stream info is available but the names are perhaps somewhat obscured," then adding last names back "once we set the proper user expectation."

The judgment goes to the business model itself. One expert testified that Facebook "sell[s] everything but your name," and a company witness confirmed that the advertising platform requires user data to function — and that users can neither stop Facebook's collection of their data nor turn off ads. The court concluded the misrepresentations "were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook's business model."

The most detailed findings concern what Facebook promised after the Cambridge Analytica revelations in March 2018 — and what it actually did. The company publicly committed to investigate every app with access to large amounts of user data, conduct full audits of suspicious apps, ban developers misusing data, ensure improperly obtained data was deleted, and notify affected users.

The court found the resulting App Developer Investigation "willfully ineffective." Over three years, Facebook conducted only 14 forensic data "audits" — and even those were known to be inadequate, with the auditor expressly disclaiming any independent verification of what developers reported. Internal materials identified about 116 developers, covering roughly 125,000 apps, that Facebook ultimately banned. On deletion, the company's own documents acknowledged there was "no reasonable enforcement/verification approach" and that the policy goal was in part "to optimize for external optics."

On notification, the gap is stark: Facebook told users of only two apps that misuse had occurred. Its investigation had identified at least 2,000 apps associated with data misuse that should have triggered notifications — including 234 apps engaged in bulk collection of friends' data and 671 that kept friends'-data access after the cutoff. The company deliberately narrowed its internal definition of data misuse so it would not have to notify as many people, "due to the operational burden of doing so." Of the misusing apps, 1,585 could be tied to New Mexico accounts, affecting at least 1,146,225 New Mexicans — more than 80% of Facebook's New Mexico user base. Facebook shut the investigation down in March 2021 without telling the public it had ended.

The findings also cover content moderation. Internal research showed Facebook's systems recommending groups and pages containing known misinformation, and its CrossCheck system letting policy-violating content from high-profile accounts stay up for an average of twelve days. In one internal exchange, an executive withheld information about hate-speech enforcement failures from a news outlet, and Sandberg replied: "This is awesome."

The judge found "substantial aggravating circumstances" — the scale, duration, repetition, breadth and willfulness of the violations, plus the involvement of senior leadership — that supported the maximum $5,000 per violation. He then reduced the total on proportionality and due-process grounds, the same constitutional concern the state's own lawyer had flagged when asking for $35–40 billion rather than the full $219.5 billion.

Meta's main proportionality argument — that it already paid $5 billion to the FTC — was rejected outright. The court ruled that settlement "cannot be viewed in a vacuum," noting the FTC's docket including subsequent litigation over violations of those very agreements. In the judge's words: "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices."

Meta will appeal. Its chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, said the company is confident it will prevail, calling the ruling one that makes it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico" and describing the lawsuit as an attempt "to impose a tax on speech." Attorney General Raúl Torrez countered that the judgment should be "a clear warning to everyone in big tech" — and noted that New Mexico, unlike nearly every other state, refused to settle and took the case to trial.

Investors should not confuse this penalty with the one already on Meta's books. The $9.89 billion legal charge that held Meta's third-quarter profit to $9.86 billion came from a separate August agreement with 52 state attorneys general over teen mental-health litigation, a framework providing for payments of up to about $18.59 billion. The $25 billion New Mexico judgment is additional, unaccrued, and — for now — unpaid, with the 15% interest clock running while the appeal proceeds.

The appeal. Meta's challenge will test two things: whether executive statements about privacy and content moderation are protected speech, and whether stacking per-violation penalties into the tens of billions survives due-process review. The company has shown it will litigate for years — the interest meter is the price of that strategy.

Injunctive relief. The court reserved the question pending further briefing. A penalty is a number; an injunction could compel changes to how Facebook collects data, vets developers, or enforces its rules — remedies the judge noted cannot be modeled in advance, which is precisely why they matter.
The fourth quarter. Meta has not accrued the $25 billion. Watch whether its Q4 accounts recognize any portion of it, and how management frames the exposure on the next earnings call.

The copycats. New Mexico was the holdout; other attorneys general settled. A $25 billion verdict — even one cut from $219.5 billion — reprices what "take it to trial" means, and every statehouse with a consumer-protection statute just took notice.

headline: US critical minerals forecast: Fodere’s test is usable output
headings: What changed, and what remains conditional
Seven tons a day is not seven tons of saleable minerals
Titanium’s opportunity is mainly industrial, not aerospace
Vanadium already has a recycling industry to compete with
Three outcomes to watch without inventing a launch date
The evidence that would change this forecast
Comments
paragraphs: Editorial illustration adapted from a rutile specimen photograph by Nessa Eull / GeoDIL (CC0 1.0), with TECHi branding. It does not depict Fodere’s facility or output.

Fodere’s new Mississippi announcement gives the U.S. critical-minerals supply chain a specific place to watch. It does not yet give manufacturers a dependable new source of titanium or vanadium. The forecast turns on what the proposed prototype can produce consistently, at a specification somebody will buy, and at a cost that survives beyond demonstration funding.

In an announcement issued at 6:42 p.m. EDT on October 19, 2026 , Fodere Critical Minerals identified Monroe County, Mississippi, for its proposed U.S. prototype. The company said it had agreed terms for an option on approximately 56 acres and was seeking up to $75 million in federal support. That is a site-development and financing signal, not a grant award or an operating plant. Fodere’s announcement makes clear that funding selection is not assured.

TECHi’s forecast: the project’s next meaningful advance will be evidence of repeatable, customer-qualified production rather than a larger capacity headline. Until that evidence appears, a prudent supply forecast should treat its contribution as prospective. The announcement supports closer monitoring; it does not support adding a specific quantity to available U.S. supply.

Fodere’s proposed process would recover useful minerals from industrial residues. Its initial product plans include synthetic rutile-grade titanium dioxide and vanadium pentoxide, with the product mix depending on the material processed. The newly disclosed site arrangements and federal funding request make the development pathway more concrete. They do not establish a commissioning date, a complete financing package or sustained operating performance.

An option matters because it can secure a route to a site while diligence proceeds. It remains different from completed acquisition, environmental clearance and permission to operate. Likewise, the requested federal support is a potential financing source. Readers should not turn “seeking up to” into “receiving,” or assume the requested amount represents the project’s total cost.

Those distinctions change the forecast. A grant decision could reduce one obstacle without resolving the others. Conversely, the company says its plans are not dependent on that award. A failed funding application would therefore be a setback to the disclosed funding route, rather than proof that the entire project had been cancelled. Financing and technical readiness need separate evidence.

On its separate pre-commercial plant page , Fodere describes a seven-ton-per-day Mississippi facility intended to validate the process before wider commercialization. The page identifies operating performance, product quality, resource use and customer feedback as objectives. It does not provide a sufficiently detailed material balance to convert the stated plant scale into annual shipments of each finished product.

That missing bridge is central to the story. A plant can process a substantial amount of material while recovering a much smaller amount of its commercially valuable constituent. The useful calculation starts with the amount and composition of the incoming material, then applies recovery rates, operating availability and the proportion of output that meets the buyer’s specification.

Consider an explicitly hypothetical example: 100 units of feed containing 10 units of a target mineral, processed at 80% recovery, would yield eight units of recovered mineral content. It would not yield 80 units. This is an illustration of the arithmetic, not a prediction of Fodere’s feed composition or performance. Chemical conversion, impurities and final product specifications would require additional accounting.

For that reason, annualizing a plant’s daily headline figure would create false precision here. The company must first explain exactly what the figure measures, how consistently it can operate and how much qualifying product emerges. A useful future disclosure would show a representative run duration, incoming composition, recovered output, rejected material and saleable yield together.

Titanium can evoke aircraft and defense hardware. The actual U.S. market for titanium mineral concentrates is much broader and less glamorous. The U.S. Geological Survey’s 2026 Mineral Commodity Summaries , in its titanium mineral concentrates chapter, estimates 88% U.S. net import reliance in 2025 . It also says more than 95% of domestic consumption went to titanium dioxide pigment producers.

Those pigments serve products such as coatings, paper and plastics. This makes industrial purchasing requirements central to the forecast. A proposed source of synthetic rutile-grade material could matter to processors, but it should not be described as a new source of finished aerospace titanium, or assumed to be ready-made pigment.

The USGS explanation of titanium’s uses also highlights the importance of purity and particle characteristics to pigment performance. Different stages of the supply chain have different requirements. Recovering titanium-bearing material is therefore only one step toward serving a particular downstream customer.

The commercial question is whether the proposed output can enter an existing purchasing and processing system reliably. Buyers will need to assess consistency, impurities, handling, logistics and processing compatibility. A sample meeting a specification once would be encouraging; repeat deliveries meeting it would be stronger evidence. The forecast improves when product qualification becomes a demonstrated operating capability.

Vanadium provides a second test of the project's commercial positioning. The same USGS report estimates U.S. vanadium net import reliance at 41% in 2025 and says metallurgical uses accounted for more than 90% of reported domestic consumption. A forecast framed exclusively around flow batteries would therefore overlook the largest existing domestic demand base.

The report also estimates 7,500 metric tons of U.S. secondary vanadium production in 2025. Existing producers recover it from materials including petroleum residues, spent catalysts and ash. Fodere’s opportunity should consequently be judged against an established industrial activity, not a claim that recovering vanadium from residues is unprecedented.

The distinction is useful for readers assessing the company’s competitive prospects. Its particular combination of feedstocks, recovery steps, products and economics would need to deliver an advantage. That might ultimately be better recovery, access to suitable material, lower costs or an attractive product mix. The announcement does not yet establish which advantage will survive at commercial scale.

Nor is vanadium pentoxide automatically equivalent to battery-ready electrolyte. Further processing and customer qualification can matter. The relevant question is who is willing to buy the actual proposed product, on what specification and under what delivery terms. Announced production ambitions alone do not answer it.

The most defensible central case is continued development rather than an immediate supply contribution. Site diligence, permitting, financing and process validation remain necessary steps. Without a disclosed, credible commissioning schedule, assigning a calendar year to commercial shipments would imply knowledge the available evidence does not provide.

An upside case would require several developments to reinforce one another: secure financing, an executable site and permitting plan, sustained operating data, and customer qualification of the resulting products. A funding announcement alone would strengthen the financing case. Repeated qualifying output, accompanied by credible purchasing commitments, would strengthen the supply case much more directly.

A downside case need not involve a spectacular technical failure. It could emerge if variable feed composition raises treatment costs, if useful products need more refining than expected, or if qualification takes longer than the funding runway allows. These are analytical conditions to monitor, not allegations that any of them has occurred at Fodere.

There is also a mixed outcome: a technically workable process that supports a smaller or different commercial business than the initial narrative suggests. One product could prove more attractive than another. A narrower feedstock range might produce better consistency. A credible forecast must leave room for that possibility instead of forcing the project into a binary success-or-failure story.

The first decisive technical disclosure would connect incoming material to outgoing products across a meaningful operating campaign. It should identify the feedstock, run duration, recovery performance and product specifications. Publishing only the best sample would leave readers unable to judge consistency; reporting a range and explaining variability would be more informative.

The next commercial disclosure would explain the relationship between qualification and revenue. A customer testing material is useful evidence of interest. A purchase commitment with defined quality and delivery obligations provides a different level of support. Neither should be confused with recurring sales from a fully operating plant.

Finally, an economic case needs more than the value of minerals in the feed. It must account for energy, reagents, transport, labor, maintenance and treatment of remaining material, alongside the capital required to build and operate the facility. Selling several products could improve the economics, but those revenues cannot simply be assumed before specifications and buyers are established.

That distinction between an announced pathway and dependable output also appears in TECHi’s Indiana power forecast . Infrastructure becomes useful supply through financed, permitted and operating assets. For Fodere, the sharper question is chemical as well as financial: can this particular residue-to-product process repeatedly make what customers need? Mississippi now has a more specific project to assess. The next evidence should establish what it can reliably deliver.

Recovering titanium-bearing material is therefore only one step toward serving a particular downstream customer. The commercial question is whether the proposed output can enter an existing purchasing and processing system reliably. Buyers will need to assess consistency, impurities, handling, logistics and processing compatibility. A sample meeting a specification once would be encouraging; repeat deliveries meeting it would be stronger evidence. The forecast improves when product qualification becomes a demonstrated operating capability. Vanadium provides a second test of the project's commercial positioning. The same USGS report estimates U.S. vanadium net import reliance at 41% in 2025 and says metallurgical uses accounted for more than 90% of reported domestic consumption. A forecast framed exclusively around flow batteries would therefore overlook the largest existing domestic demand base. The report also estimates 7,500 metric tons of U.S. secondary vanadium production in 2025. Existing producers recover it from materials including petroleum residues, spent catalysts and ash. Fodere’s opportunity should consequently be judged against an established industrial activity, not a claim that recovering vanadium from residues is unprecedented. The distinction is useful for readers assessing the company’s competitive prospects. Its particular combination of feedstocks, recovery steps, products and economics would need to deliver an advantage. That might ultimately be better recovery, access to suitable material, lower costs or an attractive product mix. The announcement does not yet establish which advantage will survive at commercial scale. Nor is vanadium pentoxide automatically equivalent to battery-ready electrolyte. Further processing and customer qualification can matter. The relevant question is who is willing to buy the actual proposed product, on what specification and under what delivery terms. Announced production ambitions alone do not answer it. The most defensible central case is continued development rather than an immediate supply contribution. Site diligence, permitting, financing and process validation remain necessary steps. Without a disclosed, credible commissioning schedule, assigning a calendar year to commercial shipments would imply knowledge the available evidence does not provide. An upside case would require several developments to reinforce one another: secure financing, an executable site and permitting plan, sustained operating data, and customer qualification of the resulting products. A funding announcement alone would strengthen the financing case. Repeated qualifying output, accompanied by credible purchasing commitments, would strengthen the supply case much more directly. A downside case need not involve a spectacular technical failure. It could emerge if variable feed composition raises treatment costs, if useful products need more refining than expected, or if qualification takes longer than the funding runway allows. These are analytical conditions to monitor, not allegations that any of them has occurred at Fodere. There is also a mixed outcome: a technically workable process that supports a smaller or different commercial business than the initial narrative suggests. One product could prove more attractive than another. A narrower feedstock range might produce better consistency. A credible forecast must leave room for that possibility instead of forcing the project into a binary success-or-failure story. The first decisive technical disclosure would connect incoming material to outgoing products across a meaningful operating campaign. It should identify the feedstock, run duration, recovery performance and product specifications. Publishing only the best sample would leave readers unable to judge consistency; reporting a range and explaining variability would be more informative. The next commercial disclosure would explain the relationship between qualification and revenue. A customer testing material is useful evidence of interest. A purchase commitment with defined quality and delivery obligations provides a different level of support. Neither should be confused with recurring sales from a fully operating plant. Finally, an economic case needs more than the value of minerals in the feed. It must account for energy, reagents, transport, labor, maintenance and treatment of remaining material, alongside the capital required to build and operate the facility. Selling several products could improve the economics, but those revenues cannot simply be assumed before specifications and buyers are established. That distinction between an announced pathway and dependable output also appears in TECHi’s Indiana power forecast . Infrastructure becomes useful supply through financed, permitted and operating assets. For Fodere, the sharper question is chemical as well as financial: can this particular residue-to-product process repeatedly make what customers need? Mississippi now has a more specific project to assess. The next evidence should establish what it can reliably deliver. headline: Indiana nuclear power forecast: gas may arrive before 6 GW
headings: What the Indiana nuclear agreement changes
The gas bridge is the forecast’s most important detail
How much electricity could 6 GW actually produce?
The NRC record shows preparation, not a construction approval
AI demand supports the opportunity, not a guaranteed buyer
Indiana’s existing sites offer a starting point, not a shortcut
Three scenarios for the Indiana power outlook
Comments
paragraphs: TECHi editorial illustration using the official AtkinsRéalis wordmark. Company marks remain their owners’ trademarks; the illustration does not imply endorsement.

Indiana’s new nuclear proposal carries a more immediate signal for the power market: gas generation may come first. AtkinsRéalis, the state and Hoosier Energy have signed an agreement to explore up to eight CANDU reactors with as much as 6 gigawatts of capacity. The evaluation also includes smaller gas plants ahead of the nuclear buildout.

That sequencing changes the Indiana nuclear power forecast. The headline number describes a possible long-term destination; it does not establish electricity available to a factory or data center on a particular date. TECHi’s assessment is that the next meaningful forecast upgrade should come from a funded site, contracted customers and a credible delivery schedule—not another increase in proposed megawatts.

The announcement, issued at 5:08 p.m. Eastern on October 19 , is a memorandum of understanding to evaluate potential deployment. It sets no firm operating date, construction budget or named AI customer. Financing, offtake arrangements, licensing, environmental review and grid connections remain dependencies.

Those omissions do not make the agreement meaningless. Bringing a technology supplier, a state government and a wholesale electricity cooperative into the same evaluation creates a route to answering practical questions together. It can align a reactor proposal with customers and infrastructure. But cooperation is an early development asset, not evidence that lenders have accepted construction risk or buyers have accepted a power price.

The distinction matters to anyone comparing competing power announcements. A capacity target measures ambition. A signed electricity contract measures a buyer’s willingness to pay under specified terms. A construction decision shows that somebody is prepared to fund the project. Operating output proves the system can deliver. Each step removes a different uncertainty, and none should be silently substituted for the next.

The partners are considering smaller simple-cycle or combined-cycle gas plants before the reactors, including possible gas-to-nuclear development at retired or retiring generation sites. No gas capacity total or delivery deadline is disclosed.

For a customer deciding where to build, that creates two separate investment questions. The first is how to secure electricity for the initial facility. The second is whether a future nuclear supply arrangement offers better long-term economics, reliability or emissions performance. A developer might find the first proposition attractive even while the second remains unresolved.

The commercial test is therefore whether the bridge works on its own. If a gas project needs a future nuclear project to justify its financing, delays in the reactor program could also weaken the earlier phase. Conversely, independently financeable generation with committed customers could serve demand even if the nuclear campus changes size. These are possible financing structures, not arrangements the parties have announced.

A bridge also needs an exit strategy. Future disclosures should explain whether gas assets would continue operating alongside reactors, be repurposed or face a shortened economic life. Without that information, readers cannot calculate the cost of transition or assume that early gas investment automatically becomes useful nuclear infrastructure. Sharing land is different from sharing every piece of equipment.

This is the same analytical distinction behind TECHi’s examination of the SLB–Liberty data-center power alliance : a plausible industrial combination becomes financially measurable only when the customer, scope and payment obligations become visible.

Gigawatts measure generating capacity; terawatt-hours measure energy produced over time. If the entire proposed 6 GW were eventually built and averaged a 90% capacity factor for a full year, it would generate approximately 47.3 TWh . The calculation is 6 GW × 8,760 hours × 0.90, divided by 1,000 to express the result in TWh.

The 90% figure here is an illustrative assumption, not a performance commitment from the partners. At an assumed 80%, the same nameplate capacity would yield about 42.0 TWh; at 95%, about 49.9 TWh. These figures describe a fully commissioned fleet in a normal 365-day year. They do not account for a staged opening, transmission losses or contractual allocation among customers.

That distinction prevents two forecasting errors. First, a campus built in phases would not contribute its eventual annual output from the first reactor’s opening. Second, annual energy is not a guarantee that a particular customer can draw its full required load every hour. Outages, network constraints and the terms of the supply contract still matter.

It would also be premature to divide the headline capacity by the reactor count and present the result as a selected unit design. Both figures are upper bounds in an evaluation. A credible model needs the actual configuration, commissioning sequence and expected operating assumptions before it can turn the campus concept into annual supply.

There is independent evidence that regulatory preparation is underway. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s August 27 meeting notice describes a pre-submittal discussion of the Enhanced CANDU 6 quality-assurance program. That supports the existence of regulatory engagement; it does not approve an Indiana plant.

The NRC’s explanation of pre-application topical reports makes the boundary clear. These reports allow particular safety-related subjects to be reviewed separately from a specific license application. Approved reports can subsequently be incorporated by reference, subject to their conditions. Review timing depends on the scope and complexity of the material.

For the forecast, the useful progression is from engagement to accepted submissions, completed technical reviews and the approvals applicable to an actual project. Counting a meeting as a license would skip the central uncertainty. Counting every preparatory step as worthless would miss genuine progress. The appropriate question is which specific uncertainty a document resolves, and which requirements still remain.

The demand backdrop is substantial but uncertain. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s U.S. data-center energy report, updated in June 2026 , models a reference case of 649 TWh of U.S. data-center electricity use in 2030 . Its compounded uncertainty cases span 521–843 TWh . These are modeled scenarios, not contracted consumption or a probability interval.

That range is a reason to investigate additional supply. It is not evidence that a particular Indiana project has secured demand. National consumption can grow while individual campuses are delayed, relocate or choose different power arrangements. A reactor developer needs commitments in the place and period where its electricity will become available, at a price sufficient to support the investment.

The strongest future signal would be an identifiable buyer taking a durable obligation: a minimum purchase, a long contract term or a clear contribution to dedicated infrastructure. A nonbinding expression of interest answers a different question. It demonstrates attention, while leaving the risk of a customer’s changed plans largely unresolved.

Readers should also avoid translating electricity demand directly into an AtkinsRéalis earnings forecast. The announcement does not disclose a project contract value or a revenue-recognition schedule. Engineering work, equipment, construction management and operating services can have different timing and economics. Potential industry demand is not the same as revenue attributable to one supplier.

Indiana’s Office of Energy Development nuclear overview says work with Purdue identified eight retired coal-plant sites as promising nuclear infrastructure candidates. That is a separate planning exercise: eight candidate sites must not be confused with the eight reactors contemplated in the new agreement. The announcement does not designate those eight locations as its selected campus sites.

Existing energy sites can make a proposal worth studying because land, a workforce and grid infrastructure may already exist. The value still depends on site-specific suitability. A prior generating connection is not proof that the network can accept any proposed replacement capacity without upgrades, and a community’s experience with one kind of plant does not settle its views on another.

Cost allocation deserves equal attention. A project could serve a major new customer while requiring infrastructure used by the wider system. The critical questions are who pays upfront, who guarantees recovery if demand disappoints, and which obligations survive a customer’s departure. Those contract terms will tell households more about their exposure than a headline promising affordable power.

There is a concrete Indiana benchmark for that disclosure. AES Indiana says its separate Google agreement has a minimum 15-year term and makes Google responsible for its power costs and required new infrastructure. The utility describes financial assurances, minimum demand commitments and exit provisions. Those are AES’s descriptions of a different project, not terms of the CANDU proposal, and Google is not identified as a buyer for the proposed reactors. They nevertheless show the kinds of contractual protections readers can look for as this evaluation develops.

TECHi’s base case is a development-stage program in which site studies, commercial negotiations and regulatory work provide the next evidence. The announced nuclear capacity should remain outside a committed-supply forecast until there is a documented basis for including it. That is a modeling discipline, not a prediction that the project will fail.

In the stronger case, the partners disclose a viable site, funded work, a creditworthy power buyer and milestones consistent with the licensing process. An independently viable gas phase could support earlier demand while the nuclear proposal advances. The forecast could then add capacity in dated stages, with the assumptions visible rather than treating the full 6 GW as one event.

In the weaker case, buyer commitments, construction economics or grid requirements fail to align. The program could shrink, take longer or stop after evaluation. A gas phase could proceed independently, or neither phase could become a funded project. No defensible probability can be assigned to those outcomes from this announcement alone.

The next release that materially changes this forecast should identify who will buy the electricity, who will finance it and when a specific tranche can credibly operate . Until then, Indiana has a significant new nuclear option to investigate—and a proposed gas bridge whose commercial terms may reveal the nearer-term power story first.

headline: D.C. Circuit upholds Pentagon’s Anthropic supply-chain exclusion
headings: What the court actually upheld
The legal leap: guardrails became supply-chain behavior
Henderson’s dissent identifies the boundary problem
What the ruling does not do
Why federal AI buyers will change their contracts
The competitive effect on the AI market
What happens next
Frequently asked questions
Comments
paragraphs: A courthouse and an AI shield illustrate the court’s decision on the Pentagon’s Anthropic supply-chain exclusion. TECHi illustration.
Illustration: A courthouse and an AI shield represent the court’s decision on the Pentagon’s Anthropic supply-chain exclusion. TECHi illustration.

The most consequential part of the D.C. Circuit’s new Anthropic ruling is easy to miss. The court did not decide whether Claude should be allowed to select military targets, nor did it endorse mass domestic surveillance. It decided who gets the last word when an AI supplier’s guardrails collide with the Pentagon’s demand for software that will perform every lawful military use.

In a 2–1 decision issued on September 25, a panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit denied Anthropic’s petitions to overturn the Department of War’s exclusion of Claude from its supply chain. Judge Gregory Katsas, joined by Judge Neomi Rao, concluded that the department had enough evidence to treat the prospect of model restrictions interfering with an expected military function as a covered supply-chain risk. Judge Karen LeCraft Henderson dissented, arguing that Congress wrote a narrower law aimed at sabotage and covert manipulation, not a supplier’s openly stated limits.

That split matters beyond one contract. It gives federal agencies a powerful procurement theory for frontier AI: a model’s behavior, including restrictions designed into it before delivery, can be treated as a supply-chain issue when the agency believes those restrictions could make a larger system fail to operate as intended.

The case is Anthropic PBC v. United States Department of War , consolidated under docket numbers 26-1049 and 26-1162. According to the 51-page opinion , the dispute arose after the department demanded contractual permission to use Claude for “all lawful uses.” Anthropic would not remove two restrictions: fully autonomous weapons that take humans out of the targeting loop, and mass surveillance of Americans.

Anthropic’s February 26 statement argued that current frontier models were not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons and that AI-enabled mass surveillance threatened civil liberties. The company nevertheless said it supported a broad range of defense applications, including foreign intelligence, operational planning and cyber operations.

The department’s position was operational rather than philosophical. Its January AI strategy required models free of policies that could limit lawful military applications. The record also described earlier cases in which commercial versions of Claude refused government prompts involving classified materials and sensitive public-health research. Anthropic developed Claude Gov and worked with government users to address those problems, but the incidents showed that model training could change what the software would do.

The confrontation sharpened in February. Secretary Pete Hegseth demanded the “all lawful uses” term on February 24. Anthropic publicly refused on February 26, following the weapons-policy standoff TECHi had tracked in Anthropic’s challenge to the Pentagon’s AI demand . On March 3, Hegseth formally determined that Claude presented a supply-chain risk under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act, or FASCSA. The department ordered the removal of Anthropic products as soon as practical, with a 180-day outside deadline, and prohibited contractors from using Claude in work performed for the department.

The majority upheld three connected determinations: that removing Claude was necessary to reduce a national-security supply-chain risk, that less intrusive measures were not reasonably available, and that the department could act immediately before completing the ordinary notice process. It also rejected Anthropic’s Fifth Amendment due-process and First Amendment retaliation claims.

FASCSA authorizes covered procurement actions when information technology creates a risk that someone may sabotage, introduce unwanted functions, extract data or otherwise manipulate a product’s design or operation so as to deny, disrupt or manipulate its use. The majority read “manipulate” broadly enough to include restrictions that Anthropic knowingly trains into Claude before delivering a new model.

The opinion emphasized that Anthropic can shape how Claude responds through model training, technical controls and contract terms. Anthropic said it has no remote “kill switch” and cannot alter a model after it has been delivered into a classified environment. The majority accepted that point, yet found it incomplete: each new version still arrives with behavior shaped by Anthropic, and the model can sit inside a larger defense system whose function depends on Claude’s responses.

That is the ruling’s durable procurement lesson. A vendor does not need a hidden backdoor or post-deployment access to create a supply-chain risk under the majority’s reasoning. If a supplier controls the design of a component and the agency reasonably fears that the component may decline an expected task, the agency can treat that behavior as a risk to the surrounding system.

The panel also deferred heavily to the executive branch on national security. It said the court could not substitute its policy judgment for the department’s assessment of how an AI model might behave during a military operation. That deference carried through the analysis of narrower alternatives. Instead of auditing every contractor and every possible use, the department was allowed to make what the majority called a “clean break.”

Judge Henderson’s dissent attacked the statutory interpretation at its foundation. In her reading, the verbs Congress chose—sabotage, maliciously introduce, extract and manipulate—describe deceptive or hostile interference with a technology supply chain. Anthropic’s restrictions were public, contractual and central to its negotiations with the government. Treating that conduct as manipulation, she wrote, stretches a security statute past the kind of covert supply-chain compromise it was designed to address.

This is more than a semantic disagreement. The majority’s approach can apply to any AI company whose model includes a refusal layer, safety classifier, policy constraint or capability limitation that a federal customer considers incompatible with its mission. The dissent would keep the statute focused on hidden or underhanded compromise and leave an openly negotiated disagreement to ordinary procurement law.

The 2–1 split therefore creates a real appeal issue. Anthropic could seek rehearing by the full D.C. Circuit or ask the Supreme Court to review the case. Whether either court would take it is uncertain, but the dissent gives the company a defined statutory argument rather than only a policy objection.
The decision is narrower than a blanket ban on Claude.

Anthropic itself drew that boundary in a March 5 customer update , saying the designation could not reach a contractor’s unrelated commercial use of Claude. That statement came as Anthropic revived talks around its $200 million military AI agreement . The court’s description of the March 6 implementation memo likewise ties the contractor restriction to work for the department.

That distinction is especially important for cloud distribution. Earlier in the dispute, Microsoft said Claude would remain available to commercial and non-defense government customers, a position TECHi covered in its report on Microsoft’s Anthropic access decision . The new opinion does not convert that Pentagon-specific restriction into a general federal or private-sector prohibition.
The practical effect will show up first in contract language and model testing.

Federal buyers are likely to demand clearer disclosure of refusal behavior, model-level safety constraints and the process for changing those constraints. “All lawful use” clauses may become more common in defense procurement, but a phrase that broad still leaves operational questions: who determines that a use is lawful, what happens when a model refuses by mistake, and how quickly must a supplier produce a corrected version?

Contractors will also need to map where a frontier model sits inside a larger system. The majority repeatedly focused on the possibility that Claude could limit the function of an application layered around it. A prime contractor that treats a general-purpose model as a replaceable API may discover that the government views the model as a mission-critical component with its own supply-chain obligations.

Testing will have to cover refusals, not only accuracy and security. A benchmark showing that a model can summarize intelligence is different from an acceptance test showing that the deployed version will respond consistently to the agency’s lawful prompts. The record cited early refusals involving violent classified material and infectious-disease research, even though Anthropic said those glitches were resolved. Under the court’s logic, a resolved refusal still proves that supplier-designed behavior can constrain a government workflow.

The decision may also favor vendors willing to build government-specific models and terms. Anthropic had already created Claude Gov and a government addendum, as described in both the opinion and its earlier government-access announcement . The dispute was not about whether customization was possible. It was about whether a supplier could retain two non-negotiable limits after the department declared them incompatible with its strategy.

The immediate beneficiary is not automatically the company with the strongest general benchmark score. It is the provider whose technical controls and contract posture most closely match the customer’s mission.

The opinion says the department moved to expand its relationship with OpenAI after beginning Claude’s removal. That detail shows how policy architecture can become a competitive product feature. In national-security procurement, a model’s permissible-use envelope can matter as much as latency, context length or reasoning performance.

Microsoft, Amazon and Google face a related distribution problem. Each can make multiple model families available through its cloud, but a government authorization does not override a model maker’s terms or an agency’s procurement exclusion. Anthropic’s prior approvals for Claude on Amazon Bedrock government workloads and Google Cloud’s authorized environments established that Claude could meet demanding infrastructure standards. The D.C. Circuit case shows that infrastructure compliance and behavioral acceptability are separate gates.

That distinction is the TECHi angle the headlines miss: the government AI market now has two supply chains. One is physical and operational—cloud regions, access controls, software dependencies and model delivery. The other is behavioral—the model’s training, refusal rules and the supplier’s authority to define acceptable use. The majority treated the second as legally part of the first.

The panel denied Anthropic’s petitions rather than sending the matter back for a narrower remedy. Unless the ruling is reheard, stayed or reversed, the department’s exclusion remains in place on the terms described in the record.

The next signals to watch are concrete. Anthropic must decide whether to seek rehearing or Supreme Court review. The department and its contractors must complete the transition away from Claude in covered work. Rival AI providers will have to show that their models can satisfy military acceptance testing without producing a different set of safety or reliability problems. Contract drafters across the government will study the opinion’s broad reading of “manipulate.”

The unresolved policy question is harder than the legal holding. The most consequential part of the D.C. Circuit’s new Anthropic ruling is easy to miss. The court did not decide whether Claude should be allowed to select military targets, nor did it endorse mass domestic surveillance. It decided who gets the last word when an AI supplier’s guardrails collide with the Pentagon’s demand for software that will perform every lawful military use. In a 2–1 decision issued on September 25, a panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit denied Anthropic’s petitions to overturn the Department of War’s exclusion of Claude from its supply chain. Judge Gregory Katsas, joined by Judge Neomi Rao, concluded that the department had enough evidence to treat the prospect of model restrictions interfering with an expected military function as a covered supply-chain risk. Judge Karen LeCraft Henderson dissented, arguing that Congress wrote a narrower law aimed at sabotage and covert manipulation, not a supplier’s openly stated limits. That split matters beyond one contract. It gives federal agencies a powerful procurement theory for frontier AI: a model’s behavior, including restrictions designed into it before delivery, can be treated as a supply-chain issue when the agency believes those restrictions could make a larger system fail to operate as intended. The case is Anthropic PBC v. United States Department of War , consolidated under docket numbers 26-1049 and 26-1162. According to the 51-page opinion , the dispute arose after the department demanded contractual permission to use Claude for “all lawful uses.” Anthropic would not remove two restrictions: fully autonomous weapons that take humans out of the targeting loop, and mass surveillance of Americans. Anthropic’s February 26 statement argued that current frontier models were not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons and that AI-enabled mass surveillance threatened civil liberties. The company nevertheless said it supported a broad range of defense applications, including foreign intelligence, operational planning and cyber operations. The department’s position was operational rather than philosophical. Its January AI strategy required models free of policies that could limit lawful military applications. The record also described earlier cases in which commercial versions of Claude refused government prompts involving classified materials and sensitive public-health research. Anthropic developed Claude Gov and worked with government users to address those problems, but the incidents showed that model training could change what the software would do. The confrontation sharpened in February. Secretary Pete Hegseth demanded the “all lawful uses” term on February 24. Anthropic publicly refused on February 26, following the weapons-policy standoff TECHi had tracked in Anthropic’s challenge to the Pentagon’s AI demand . On March 3, Hegseth formally determined that Claude presented a supply-chain risk under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act, or FASCSA. The department ordered the removal of Anthropic products as soon as practical, with a 180-day outside deadline, and prohibited contractors from using Claude in work performed for the department. The majority upheld three connected determinations: that removing Claude was necessary to reduce a national-security supply-chain risk, that less intrusive measures were not reasonably available, and that the department could act immediately before completing the ordinary notice process. It also rejected Anthropic’s Fifth Amendment due-process and First Amendment retaliation claims. FASCSA authorizes covered procurement actions when information technology creates a risk that someone may sabotage, introduce unwanted functions, extract data or otherwise manipulate a product’s design or operation so as to deny, disrupt or manipulate its use. The majority read “manipulate” broadly enough to include restrictions that Anthropic knowingly trains into Claude before delivering a new model. The opinion emphasized that Anthropic can shape how Claude responds through model training, technical controls and contract terms. Anthropic said it has no remote “kill switch” and cannot alter a model after it has been delivered into a classified environment. The majority accepted that point, yet found it incomplete: each new version still arrives with behavior shaped by Anthropic, and the model can sit inside a larger defense system whose function depends on Claude’s responses. If a supplier controls the design of a component and the agency reasonably fears that the component may decline an expected task, the agency can treat that behavior as a risk to the surrounding system. The panel also deferred heavily to the executive branch on national security. It said the court could not substitute its policy judgment for the department’s assessment of how an AI model might behave during a military operation. That deference carried through the analysis of narrower alternatives. Instead of auditing every contractor and every possible use, the department was allowed to make what the majority called a “clean break.” Judge Henderson’s dissent attacked the statutory interpretation at its foundation. In her reading, the verbs Congress chose—sabotage, maliciously introduce, extract and manipulate—describe deceptive or hostile interference with a technology supply chain. Anthropic’s restrictions were public, contractual and central to its negotiations with the government. Treating that conduct as manipulation, she wrote, stretches a security statute past the kind of covert supply-chain compromise it was designed to address. This is more than a semantic disagreement. The majority’s approach can apply to any AI company whose model includes a refusal layer, safety classifier, policy constraint or capability limitation that a federal customer considers incompatible with its mission. headline: OpenAI Pauses AI Model Work After Agent Escapes Its Sandbox
headings: What the OpenAI agent actually did
The pause is narrower than the headlines—and more important
The monitoring system worked, but the stop mechanism did not
Where reports about U.S. government sites fit
The deeper risk is composability
What OpenAI must prove before restarting
Government adoption raises the stakes
What happens next
Frequently asked questions
